claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy has a single-phase ordered hexagonal structure.
Post-deposition low-temperature annealing introduces controlled sub-micrometer inhomogeneities.
Annealing produces grain-boundary refinement and microstrain modulation.
Sub-micrometer inhomogeneities influence magnetic-domain nucleation and propagation during the magnetostructural transition.
Annealing increases magnetic homogeneity and homogenizes local magnetic exchange interactions.
Annealing reduces the hysteresis width and associated hysteretic losses.
Annealing makes the magnetic entropy change more gradual.
Annealing causes a slight, controllable shift in the transition temperature.
Annealing enhances thermal transport through improved microstructural features.
The as-deposited baseline has a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited baseline has a large but abrupt magnetic entropy change.
The as-deposited baseline has constrained heat-exchange rates because of a low surface-to-volume ratio.
Thin films or coatings enable rapid heat exchange because of their high surface area.
The predicted annealing effects hold under low applied magnetic fields near the transition temperature.

contradictions.description: Annealing is said to introduce inhomogeneities that govern the response, but it is also said to reduce defects and homogenize exchange interactions. The hypothesis does not distinguish beneficial engineered heterogeneity from the heterogeneity being removed.

The as-deposited baseline is assigned a low surface-to-volume ratio, whereas the proposed measurements use high-surface-area thin films or coatings. It is unclear whether baseline and annealed samples share the same geometry.
The intervention permits either annealing or substrate-induced strain engineering, but the falsification experiment tests only annealing, so it cannot falsify the strain-engineering version.
